boss.title: Weekend 1 boss: the slow sale page

situation.text: The sale page of `shop.example` loads slowly. Visitors leave before it shows. Two things go wrong:

items: Every visitor downloads the same logo again.
Visitors far away wait for each page.

sequenceDiagram

intro.title: How a page reaches you
screens: A page travels from a server to your browser.
Caches and proxies keep copies on the way, so pages load faster.
intro.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Browser --> CDN
  CDN --> Server

screens.text: Cache is a tool of the web.
A cache keeps a copy of a response, so the next visit loads faster.

catch.question: Why does a browser keep a copy of a page?
choices: To load it faster next time
To hide it from the server
catch.explanation: A saved copy can be shown without a new download.

card.text: A cache keeps a copy of a response. The next request can use the copy. This saves time and network.
card.example: Your browser shows the shop logo from its cache on the second visit.

review.question: What does a cache keep?
review.answer: A copy of a response, so the next request can skip the download.

workedExample.problem: The product page loads slowly for every visitor.
steps: Find the parts that change rarely.
Let the browser cache them for one hour.
workedExample.answer: Cache the logo and the styles. Keep the price fresh.

tradeOff.situation: Prices change every minute. The product page is slow.
options: Cache the page for one hour
Cache the page but not the price

reasons.text: The page is fast and the price stays fresh.
One hour is short enough for prices.
Caching nothing is always safest.

tradeOff.explanation: Cache what rarely changes. Fetch the price each time.

decisionCards.situation: The shop logo changes once a year.

reasons.text: A file that rarely changes can be kept for long.
No store makes it load faster.
Logos must always be fresh.

decisionCards.explanation: A long TTL saves a download on every visit.

screens.text: TTL is a tool of the web.
The time to live says how long the copy stays fresh.

catch.question: What tells a cache when a copy is too old?
catch.explanation: The time to live says how long the copy stays fresh.

card.text: TTL means time to live. It says how long a cached copy stays fresh.
card.example: max-age=3600 keeps the logo fresh for one hour.

review.question: What does TTL mean?
review.answer: Time to live: how long a copy stays fresh.

screens.text: No store is a tool of the web.
Shops use no store every day.
no-store tells every cache to keep no copy.

catch.question: Which header stops a cache from keeping a copy?
catch.explanation: no-store tells every cache to keep no copy.

card.text: no-store tells caches to keep no copy. Every request goes to the server.
card.example: A bank sends no-store on the account page.

review.question: What does no-store do?
review.answer: It tells caches to keep no copy of the response.

screens.text: Cookie is a tool of the web.
A cookie is small data the browser sends back.

catch.question: How does a server remember you between requests?
choices: It keeps the connection open forever
catch.explanation: The browser sends the cookie back with each request.

card.text: A cookie is a small piece of data. The server sends it, and the browser sends it back.
card.example: The shop keeps your cart in a cookie.

review.question: Who sends a cookie back?
review.answer: The browser, with each request to the same site.

workedExample.problem: A customer loses the cart on every page.
steps: Store a cart id in a cookie.
workedExample.answer: The cookie brings the cart id back with each request.

catch.question: What keeps page scripts from reading a cookie?
catch.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from scripts on the page.

card.text: HttpOnly hides a cookie from page scripts. The browser still sends it to the server.
card.example: The shop marks its session cookie HttpOnly.

review.question: What does HttpOnly do?
review.answer: It hides the cookie from page scripts.

catch.question: What sits between the browser and the server and passes requests on?
catch.explanation: A proxy receives the request and sends it on.

card.text: A proxy sits between the client and the server. It passes requests on and can keep copies.
card.example: A CDN is a proxy close to the visitor.

review.question: Where does a proxy sit?
review.answer: Between the client and the server.

workedExample.problem: Visitors far away wait for every page.
steps: Put a proxy close to them.
Let it keep copies of the pages.
workedExample.answer: The proxy answers from a nearby copy.

catch.question: What brings copies of a site close to visitors?
catch.explanation: A CDN keeps copies on servers near visitors.

card.text: A CDN is a group of proxies around the world. Each one keeps copies near visitors.
card.example: A visitor in Hanoi gets the logo from a server in Singapore.

review.question: What is a CDN?
review.answer: Proxies around the world that keep copies near visitors.

placement.question: What is a cookie?
placement.answer: Small data the browser sends back.

placement.question: What is a proxy?
placement.answer: A server between the client and the server.

scenarios.name: Sale day
scenarios.problem: A sale starts at noon. Ten times more people open the shop.

turns.threat: Every visitor downloads the same logo and styles again.
turns.constraint: The logo changes once a year.

reasons.text: A rarely changed file is safe to keep for long.
A long TTL makes prices fresh.
Browsers never keep logos.

moves.counterattack: The logo loads fast, but a new logo takes an hour to show.
Far visitors are faster, but each first load is still slow.
Scripts cannot read the cookie, but the page is still slow.

turns.modelAnswer: Give the logo and styles a long TTL. Browsers keep a copy, so the server sends each file once.
keyPoints: The logo and styles rarely change.
A TTL lets browsers reuse their copy.
A new logo shows only after the TTL ends.

turns.threat: The new sale price does not show. Visitors see the old price.
turns.constraint: The price changes every minute during the sale.

reasons.text: No store makes every page faster.
A price must never come from an old copy.
A CDN always has the newest price.

moves.counterattack: Prices are fresh, but each price check now reaches the server.
Near copies update sooner, but some visitors still see the old price.
The old price stays until its copy is too old.

turns.modelAnswer: Mark the price response no-store. Every visitor then gets the current price from the server.
keyPoints: A price must never come from an old copy.
No store stops every cache from keeping it.
Each price check now costs a server request.

turns.threat: Visitors far away wait three seconds for each page.
turns.constraint: Half the visitors live on another continent.

reasons.text: No store makes far pages faster.
A cookie makes the page lighter.
A copy near the visitor cuts the travel time.

moves.counterattack: Pages now load near each visitor, but the network costs more.
Every page is fetched again, so far visitors wait longer.
The cookie is safer, but far visitors still wait.

turns.modelAnswer: Put a CDN in front of the shop. Its servers near each visitor answer instead of the far origin.
keyPoints: Distance makes each request slow.
A CDN keeps copies near the visitor.
The CDN costs money for the network.

Blame protects the team.
A vague answer avoids a fight.

moves.label: Give the cause, the new date and the risk.
moves.counterattack: The client trusts the new date.

moves.label: Say the server team was slow.
moves.counterattack: The client now doubts the whole team.

moves.label: Say it will be ready soon.
moves.counterattack: The client asks again tomorrow.

turns.modelAnswer: Say what went wrong, the new date and the one risk left.
keyPoints: Name the cause.

scenarios.name: Cache diff
scenarios.problem: An agent added caching to the price endpoint.

turns.threat: The price response is now cached for one hour.
turns.constraint: The release goes out tonight.

reasons.text: A cached price shows shoppers the wrong amount.
Caching always makes an API safer.
A test is never needed for headers.

moves.counterattack: The release waits, but no old price reaches a shopper.
Shoppers see old prices for an hour.
A test finds it, but the release is late.

turns.modelAnswer: Block it. A price must never be cached for an hour.
keyPoints: The price must stay fresh.
One hour of old prices is a real loss.
Ask for no-store on prices.

scenarios.name: Public API launch
scenarios.problem: The shop opens its API to every partner on Monday.

turns.threat: One partner sends 500 requests each second and slows everyone.

moves.counterattack: The partner slows down, but its big jobs take longer.
The partner gets a new key and sends just as much.
Some answers come from copies, but the writes still pile up.

turns.modelAnswer: Give each partner a quota. One partner can then never use all the capacity.
keyPoints: One client can use all the capacity.
A quota caps each client.
Big jobs now take longer.

turns.threat: A leaked API key is used from an unknown server.

moves.counterattack: The leaked key stops working, but the partner must update its key.
The stranger is slower, but it still reads data.
Scripts cannot read the cookie, but the key still works.

turns.modelAnswer: Rotate the leaked key at once. The old key stops working, and the partner gets a new one.
keyPoints: A leaked key works for anyone.
Rotation makes the old key useless.
The partner must update its key.

turns.threat: A partner retries every failed call at once, and the load comes back.

moves.counterattack: The retries wait their turn, but the partner sees more errors.
The key changes, but the retries keep coming.
The copies do not help, because every retry is new.

turns.modelAnswer: Keep the quota and answer 429 with a wait time. The partner then retries later.
keyPoints: Retries at once bring the load back.
The quota still protects the API.
The partner sees more errors.
